item.title: Station Prepares to Welcome Crew-13 while Continuing Space Research
item.dc:creator: Mark A. Garcia
item.description: Expedition 75 is getting the International Space Station ready for the arrival of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission scheduled to launch and dock to the orbital outpost on Thursday, Oct. 1. In the meantime, space research and lab maintenance rounded out the schedule keeping the astronauts and cosmonauts busy on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
Expedition 75 is getting the International Space Station ready for the arrival of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission scheduled to launch and dock to the orbital outpost on Thursday, Oct. 1. In the meantime, space research and lab maintenance rounded out the schedule keeping the astronauts and cosmonauts busy on Wednesday.

Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins and pilot Luke Delaney, both NASA astronauts, along with mission specialists Johsua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) and Sergey Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos will launch aboard a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft atop the Falcon 9 rocket at 11:10 a.m. EDT on Thursday. NASA+ begins its live launch coverage at 9:20 a.m. from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station’s Launch Pad 40 in Florida.

Dragon will dock to the Harmony module’s forward port on the orbital outpost about 7 p.m. the same day. The four Crew-13 members will open the hatch about an hour-and-a-half later, enter Harmony, and join the Expedition 75 crew for welcoming remarks and a safety orientation. Docking coverage begins at 5:20 p.m. on NASA+.

Three NASA astronauts living aboard the station worked together on Wednesday getting ready for the arrival of Crew-13. Station commander Jessica Meir reorganized cargo inside the Harmony’s pressurized mating adapter-2, where Dragon will dock, making room for Crew-13’s entry into the orbital outpost. Flight engineers Anil Menon and Jack Hathaway staged supplies in Harmony necessary to support the four crewmates immediately after their entry into the station and beginning their mission.

Flight engineer Sophie Adenot of ESA (European Space Agency) focused primarily on science throughout her shift on Wednesday. Adenot started her day in the Columbus laboratory module working out on the European Enhanced Exploration Exercise Device (E4D). She pedaled on the E4D’s exercise cycle continuing to test the device’s ability to keep crews fit inside spacecraft during long-term missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Next, she practiced simulated lunar landing techniques on a computer helping researchers understand how microgravity affects a crew member’s cognition when manually piloting a spacecraft.

Roscosmos flight engineer Andrey Fedyaev continued testing the lower body negative pressure suit that reverses space-caused fluid shifts from the head toward the feet. The specialized suit may help crews adjust quicker to Earth’s gravity after a long-term mission in weightlessness.

Roscosmos flight engineers Anna Kikina and Pyotr Dubrov took turns wearing arm, wrist, and finger cuffs measuring their blood pressure to understand how microgravity affects a crew member’s microcirculatory system. Afterward, Kikina unloaded cargo delivered recently aboard the Progress 96 cargo spacecraft while Dubrov worked on life support and computer maintenance.

item.title: Advanced Health Research Begins Week as Station Awaits Crew-13 Mission
item.dc:creator: Mark A. Garcia
item.description: Expedition 75 began the week scanning veins, checking out space workout gear, and testing specialized suits to ease the adjustment to Earth’s gravity. Back on Earth, NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 members are counting down to a launch on Oct. 1.
item.content:encoded:
Expedition 75 began the week scanning veins, checking out space workout gear, and testing specialized suits to ease the adjustment to Earth’s gravity. Back on Earth, NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 members are counting down to a launch on Oct. 1.

NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Anil Menon, station commander and flight engineer respectively, started their shift together with vein scans in the Columbus laboratory module. Meir operated the Ultrasound 3 device and scanned Menon’s jugular vein then measured his blood pressure for the Venous Flow investigation. Doctors will analyze the biomedical data to detect potential space-caused blood conditions such as blood clots or changes to blood chemistry.

NASA flight engineer Jack Hathaway assisted Menon at the beginning of the vein study collecting a blood sample and placing it inside a centrifuge for spinning. At the conclusion of the sample processing, Menon analyzed the sample for a red blood cell count to help doctors determine if the cardiovascular system, influenced by microgravity, delivers adequate oxygen throughout a crew member’s body. Afterward, Hathaway collected station water samples for microbial analysis then cleaned his crew quarters in the port side of the Harmony module.

Meir later joined the three crewmates she will return to Earth with next week and tested specialized suits that may help the foursome quickly adjust to gravity after nearly eight months in space. The suit may help maintain adequate cerebral blood pressure once on the ground and prevent dizziness or light-headedness at the end of a mission. Meir and Hathaway along with flight engineers Sophie Adenot of ESA (European Space Agency) and Andrey Fedyaev of Roscosmos are preparing to ride the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft back to Earth a few days after the SpaceX Crew-13 mission launches and docks to the orbital outpost on Thursday. Oct. 1.

Flight engineer Sophie Adenot of ESA (European Space Agency) spent most of her shift working on exercise research hardware. Adenot’s first job was inside the Tranquility module where she tested the functionality of ARED (advanced resistive exercise device) Kinematics computer hardware. The human research study allows researchers to track an astronaut’s body load during a space workout to optimize crew health in microgravity. Next, she guided Menon on how to work out on the European Enhanced Exploration Exercise Device (E4D) located in Columbus. The E4D is being evaluated for its ability to keep crews fit inside spacecraft on long-term missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Fedyaev conducted a second session with an experimental suit, this one designed by Roscosmos, that may ease his adjustment to Earth’s gravity. Roscosmos flight engineer Anna Kikina assisted Fedyaev as he wore the lower body negative pressure suit that reverses space-caused fluid shifts from the head toward the feet. Kikina also pointed a camera out a window on the Zvezda service module and photographed landmarks in southern Russia from the Volga River to the Ukok Plateau.

Roscosmos flight engineer Pyotr Dubrov explored high-purity semiconductor crystals using a high-temperature furnace in the Nauka science module. The physics research may advance space and terrestrial manufacturing techniques.
